article_units.name: Hardware and Systems
article_units.subtitle: CPU architecture, storage, embedded systems and how a computer's components work together

lessons.title: The CPU and Von Neumann Architecture
lessons.description: The purpose of the CPU and the role of the CU, ALU, registers, cache and main memory.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: CPU registers and Von Neumann are universal. Eduqas explicitly names every register (PC, CIR, ACC, MAR, MDR) — confirm AQA/OCR L1 covers all five; if not, add MAR/MDR detail. Keep Von Neumann diagram if it exists.

lessons.title: Fetch-Decode-Execute and CPU Performance
lessons.description: How the FDE cycle uses registers and what makes a CPU faster: clock speed, cores and cache.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: FDE cycle is concept-identical across all three boards. Eduqas wants candidates to map each FDE step onto the named registers (MAR/MDR/CIR/PC) — keep the step-by-step register trace from the source lesson if it exists; otherwise add.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Storage
lessons.description: RAM, ROM, flash, cache and virtual memory; magnetic, optical, solid-state and cloud secondary storage.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Storage characteristics transfer cleanly. Eduqas asks students to compare media on five named criteria (capacity, durability, portability, speed, cost) — structure the comparison table around exactly those five so practice questions align with mark-scheme phrasing.

lessons.title: Additional Hardware Components
lessons.description: The role of GPUs (integrated and dedicated), sound cards and motherboards in a computer system.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Eduqas explicitly assesses additional hardware (GPU, sound card, motherboard) as a named topic — AQA/OCR treat it more peripherally. Likely needs a focused fresh-ish lesson. Reuse any AQA/OCR motherboard or GPU explanations as reference; rewrite around the Eduqas-named trio.

lessons.title: Embedded Systems
lessons.description: What makes a system embedded and how everyday devices use embedded computers.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Identical concept across boards. Reuse examples (washing machine, traffic lights, fitness band, microwave) and characteristics list. Keep contrast with general-purpose computer.

article_units.name: Networks, the Internet and Cybersecurity
article_units.subtitle: Topologies, the 7-layer OSI model, contemporary protocols, the internet and protecting systems

lessons.title: Networks and Topologies
lessons.description: Characteristics of networks plus star, mesh, ring and bus topologies with advantages and disadvantages.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Topologies are universal. Eduqas specifically wants star and mesh compared against ring and bus — ensure all four topologies are present in the lesson body (some boards drop ring/bus).

lessons.title: Network Hardware and Standards
lessons.description: Routers, switches, hubs, bridges, WAPs and NICs, plus why networking standards exist.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Eduqas names six devices (router, hub, switch, bridge, WAP, NIC) — wider list than AQA/OCR. Add bridge and standards-rationale paragraphs if missing in source; the rest transfers.

lessons.title: The OSI 7-Layer Model and Protocols
lessons.description: Each of the 7 OSI layers and where contemporary protocols (HTTP, SMTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet, WiFi) sit.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Eduqas is the only major board that assesses the full 7-layer OSI model — AQA and OCR use TCP/IP 4/5-layer or skip layered architecture. The 2024 examiner report flagged OSI layer descriptions as a weak point. Lesson must be built fresh against OSI; protocols only partially transfer.

lessons.title: Packet Switching and Routing
lessons.description: TCP/IP packets, how packet switching works and how routers calculate costs to pick a path.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Packet switching is universal but Eduqas explicitly requires calculation of routing costs (graph traversal style), which AQA/OCR do not. Adapt source for the concept; add a fresh worked routing-cost example with a small weighted-graph diagram.

lessons.title: The Internet: DNS, URLs and the Web Browser
lessons.description: How DNS resolves names to IP addresses, the structure of a URL and what a browser does.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: DNS and URL anatomy transfer cleanly. Keep the DNS-resolution sequence (browser asks resolver → root → TLD → authoritative).

lessons.title: Cybersecurity Threats and Defences
lessons.description: Malware, phishing, social engineering, brute-force, DoS, interception and SQL injection plus the defences used against them.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Threats and defences are essentially identical across boards. Eduqas adds penetration testing and network forensics — make sure both appear as named defences. Reuse threat-defence pairing examples.

article_units.name: Data Representation and Storage
article_units.subtitle: Binary, hexadecimal, character sets, graphics, sound and compression

lessons.title: Data Types and Number Systems
lessons.description: Integer, real, character, string and Boolean data types plus denary, binary and hexadecimal conversion.
spec_references: 4. Data representation and storage — Data types
4. Data representation and storage — Representation of numbers

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Number-base conversion transfers 1:1. Combine data types and number bases here so Eduqas data type list (integer/real/character/string/Boolean) is locked in alongside the conversion drills.

lessons.title: Signed Binary, Addition, Subtraction and Shifts
lessons.description: Two's complement, sign and magnitude, binary arithmetic, overflow and arithmetic shifts.
spec_references: 4. Data representation and storage — Representation of numbers

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA covers two's complement but not sign and magnitude — Eduqas requires both. Adapt AQA's two's complement explanation; add a fresh sign-and-magnitude section with a worked comparison. Eduqas also lists arithmetic shifts (not just logical) — verify shift treatment.

lessons.title: Characters: ASCII and Unicode
lessons.description: How characters are stored as numbers and the trade-off between ASCII and Unicode.
spec_references: 4. Data representation and storage — Representation of characters
section_markers: American Standard Code for Information Interchange

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Character-set content is identical across boards. Reuse the ASCII table extract and Unicode-vs-ASCII comparison.

lessons.title: Graphics: Pixels, Resolution and Colour Depth
lessons.description: How images are stored as bitmaps and how to calculate file size from dimensions and colour depth.
spec_references: 4. Data representation and storage — Representation of graphics

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Bitmap storage and size calculation transfer cleanly. Use the same width × height × bit-depth formula and ÷8 to bytes conversion.

lessons.title: Sound: Sampling and File Size
lessons.description: How sound is digitised, the effect of sampling rate and how to calculate sound file size.
spec_references: 4. Data representation and storage — Representation of sound

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Sound sampling is consistent across boards. Sample-rate × bit-depth × duration calculation transfers directly.

lessons.title: Storage Units, Capacity and Compression
lessons.description: Bit, nibble, byte through to petabyte (base-2), capacity calculation and lossy vs lossless compression with ratios.
spec_references: 4. Data representation and storage — Storage requirements

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Eduqas specifies base-2 prefixes (1 KB = 1024 B) — AQA uses base-10 (1 KB = 1000 B). This is a real divergence. Source content needs the unit-prefix definitions rewritten for base-2; compression theory and ratio calculation transfer.

article_units.name: Logic, Data Organisation and Operating Systems
article_units.subtitle: Boolean logic and algebra, arrays and records, plus what an OS and utility software do

lessons.title: Logical Operators and Truth Tables
lessons.description: AND, OR, NOT and XOR in truth tables and how to use them to solve problems.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AND/OR/NOT/XOR truth tables are identical across boards. Reuse the four base tables and a small combined-circuit example.

lessons.title: Boolean Algebra and Simplification
lessons.description: Simplifying Boolean expressions using the identity, commutative, distribution, absorption and association rules.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Boolean algebra simplification (with the named rules in Appendix B) is unique to Eduqas at GCSE — AQA and OCR don't assess it formally until A level. 2024 examiner report flagged this as a weak area. Build fresh with worked simplifications using each of the eight named rules.

lessons.title: Data Structures: Arrays, Records and File Design
lessons.description: Designing and using 1D arrays, 2D arrays and records, and choosing the right structure for a problem.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Arrays and records transfer directly. Eduqas combines records and file design — keep the records lesson tightly coupled to a simple file scenario (e.g. student-record file) so the file-design content has a natural home.

lessons.title: Operating Systems and Utility Software
lessons.description: What the OS manages (CPU, memory, peripherals, security) and the role of common utility programs.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: OS responsibilities transfer 1:1. Eduqas lists a much longer utility software inventory (clipboard manager, system profiler, partition editor, archiver, cryptographic utilities, revision control etc.) — verify all are mentioned, even briefly, as named software.

article_units.name: Algorithms, Programming and Software Development
article_units.subtitle: Pseudocode, flowcharts, searching, sorting, validation and the software tools that build programs

lessons.title: Defining Algorithms: Pseudocode and Flowcharts
lessons.description: How to read, write and interpret algorithms using pseudocode and flowchart conventions.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Pseudocode is concept-shared but Eduqas has its OWN named pseudocode conventions in Appendix A (output literal in quotes, set keyword for assignment, for…next i syntax, declare/end subroutine, etc.) — rewrite all pseudocode examples to match Appendix A exactly. Flowchart symbols are universal.

lessons.title: Programming Constructs and Subroutines
lessons.description: Sequence, selection, iteration, subroutines, local and global variables and self-documenting code.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Constructs and subroutines are universal. Rewrite any code snippets in the Eduqas Appendix A pseudocode style. Eduqas adds rogue values as a named topic — ensure a worked sentinel-loop example.

lessons.title: Searching: Linear and Binary
lessons.description: How linear and binary search algorithms work, traced step by step on small datasets.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Linear and binary search transfer directly. Keep the side-by-side comparison and the explicit prerequisite that binary search needs sorted data.

lessons.title: Sorting: Bubble and Merge
lessons.description: How bubble sort and merge sort work, with worked traces and a note on relative efficiency.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Bubble sort transfers cleanly. OCR uses merge sort too; AQA pairs bubble with insertion. Confirm merge sort coverage (divide → merge → recombine) is fleshed out — students often understand the split but not the merge step. The 2024 Eduqas examiner report flagged sort traces as a recurring weakness.

lessons.title: Validation, Verification and High-Level Languages
lessons.description: Why we validate and verify data, common techniques, and high vs low-level programming languages.
spec_references: 7. Principles of programming — Levels of computer language
8. Algorithms and constructs — Validation and verification

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Validation techniques and language levels both transfer cleanly. Combine into one lesson since each spec topic is small. Use an example data-validation routine in Eduqas pseudocode style.

lessons.title: IDE Tools, Translators and Errors
lessons.description: What an IDE provides, the role of compilers, interpreters and assemblers, and types of programming error.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Translators and basic IDE tools transfer. Eduqas explicitly lists compilation stages (lexical, syntax, semantic, code generation, code optimisation) — AQA/OCR usually skip these at GCSE. Add a labelled compilation-pipeline diagram. Also include linking, rounding and truncation as named error types — they are Eduqas-specific extras.

article_units.name: Society, Ethics and the Law
article_units.subtitle: How digital technology affects society and the legislation that governs it

lessons.title: Ethical, Cultural, Environmental and Privacy Impacts
lessons.description: How digital technology shapes the workplace, the environment, culture and personal privacy.
spec_references: 11. Impacts of digital technology on wider society — Impacts

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Impact themes are universal. Keep balanced both-sides treatment so students can answer extended-evaluation questions (Eduqas regularly asks for opposing views).

lessons.title: Legislation and Professional Standards
lessons.description: GDPR/DPA 2018, Computer Misuse Act, Copyright, Creative Commons, RIPA, Telecoms Regs, FOI and codes of conduct.
spec_references: 11. Impacts of digital technology on wider society — Legislation
11. Impacts of digital technology on wider society — Professional standards

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: GDPR, DPA, CMA and Copyright transfer directly. Eduqas adds RIPA, Telecommunications Regulations and Freedom of Information — these need fresh paragraphs. Professional standards is an Eduqas-only named topic — write a short fresh section on BCS-style codes of conduct.

unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Eduqas has no NEA. AQA-style coursework scaffolding lessons (if any) have no Eduqas analogue.

unique_to_source.lesson: Computational thinking as a dedicated lesson
unique_to_source.why_not_in_target: Eduqas weaves computational thinking through Component 2 (decomposition, abstraction) rather than as a standalone topic. Folded into Python practice unit.

unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Eduqas is the only mainstream GCSE board to assess formal Boolean simplification (Appendix B rules) — not in AQA 8525 or OCR J277 at GCSE level.
AQA/OCR use TCP/IP 4-layer; only Eduqas requires the full 7-layer OSI model. Content built fresh.
Eduqas specifies routing cost calculations (weighted-path traversal) — AQA/OCR do not.
Eduqas spec lists explicit compilation stages (lexical/syntax/semantic/code gen/optimisation) and additional error types (linking, rounding, truncation) not found in AQA/OCR specs.
Eduqas lists RIPA, Telecommunications Regulations and Freedom of Information as named legislation — AQA/OCR focus on GDPR/CMA/Copyright only.

unique_to_target.lesson: Designing, Testing and Refining a Solution
unique_to_target.why_no_source_match: Component 2 on-screen practical is Eduqas-only at GCSE — no AQA/OCR analogue since AQA dropped NEA in 2020 and OCR has no programming exam.

question_type_names: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students learn the layer names by mnemonic but cannot describe what each layer DOES. The 2024 Eduqas examiners' report flagged OSI layer description as an area where centres should improve understanding — naming a layer scored full marks, describing its function scored partial.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Examiners' Report Summer 2024, wjec.co.uk/media/uubnvwaz/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-final-report-s24.pdf

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students apply identity and complement rules correctly but miss opportunities to use absorption or distribution, so leave expressions unsimplified. The 2024 examiners' report singled out Boolean simplification as a weak topic.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Examiners' Report Summer 2024, wjec.co.uk/media/uubnvwaz/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-final-report-s24.pdf

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students can read code but cannot produce a row-by-row trace table with the variable state after each line, especially when loops modify counters. Trace-table questions are a regular Component 1 mark sink.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Examiners' Report Summer 2024, wjec.co.uk/media/uubnvwaz/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-final-report-s24.pdf

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use base-10 prefixes (1 KB = 1000 B) imported from physics or general computing. Eduqas explicitly defines base-2 prefixes (1 KB = 1024 B); answers using base-10 are marked incorrect on calculation questions.
common_misconceptions.source: WJEC Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Specification (2020), Appendix and section 4, eduqas.co.uk/media/tf3bvmxe/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-specification-10-02-2020.pdf

common_misconceptions.topic: Cache vs RAM vs virtual memory
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name cache as 'fast' and RAM as 'main memory' but cannot explain why cache exists (CPU stalls without it) or how virtual memory uses secondary storage to extend RAM.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Guidance for Teaching, eduqas.co.uk/media/qyep4cj1/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-guidance-for-teaching.pdf

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe both as 'turning code into machine code' without distinguishing translation-then-run from line-by-line execution. They also confuse compilation stages with translator types.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Guidance for Teaching, eduqas.co.uk/media/qyep4cj1/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-guidance-for-teaching.pdf

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list 'good things' and 'bad things' in parallel without weighing them or anchoring claims to a specific technology. The 2024 examiners' report noted weak treatment of social impacts in extended-response answers.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Examiners' Report Summer 2024, wjec.co.uk/media/uubnvwaz/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-final-report-s24.pdf

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'validation' and 'verification' as synonyms. Validation checks whether data is sensible (range, type, format); verification checks whether it was entered correctly (double entry, proofreading). Lost easy marks every series.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Guidance for Teaching, eduqas.co.uk/media/qyep4cj1/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-guidance-for-teaching.pdf

student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Convert (Binary/Hex/Denary): Working is not required — only the final answer scores. Students who write the conversion table but omit the boxed answer score zero. Conversions must be to the requested base only (e.g. a hex-to-binary question should not return a decimal answer).
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Complete a Truth Table: Students fill in only the output column when both intermediate AND output columns are needed for combined-gate questions. Each output cell is independently marked — empty rows score zero even if other rows are correct.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Calculate Storage: Eduqas uses base-2 (1 KB = 1024 B). Calculations using base-10 lose the unit-conversion mark. Width × height × bit-depth gives bits — students often forget to divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for kB.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Trace an Algorithm: Students give the final value of the output variable but skip intermediate variable states. Mark scheme awards a mark for each correct row of the trace table; producing only the final answer caps the score at 1.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Simplify a Boolean Expression: Students stop at a partial simplification. Each application of a named law (identity, complement, absorption etc.) scores a mark — showing the rule used in a margin annotation maximises credit.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Compare: Students list features of A and features of B in two separate paragraphs without comparing. Each comparison point must explicitly contrast the two (e.g. 'unlike RAM, which is volatile, ROM retains data when power is removed').
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudoco: Students use a language they like (Python, JavaScript) instead of Eduqas Appendix A pseudocode. While most pseudocode is accepted, students should follow the spec conventions (set for assignment, output for literal output, for…next i for counted loops).
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Discuss Impacts: Students give one-sided answers (all negatives or all positives). The mark scheme rewards balanced reasoning and a concluding judgement. The 2024 examiners' report flagged this as a weak area at Component 1.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 1 is 100 marks, Component 2 is 80 marks. Both worth 50% — Component 2 marks are weighted upwards in the final grade.
Component 1 AO split: AO1 60 marks, AO2 30 marks, AO3 10 marks. Plan article lessons to spend more time on recall scaffolding (AO1) than on application drills.
Component 2 AO split: AO1 0 marks, AO2 40 marks, AO3 40 marks. Practice problems must include both 'apply a known technique' (AO2) and 'design/refine a solution' (AO3) styles.
Hardware, networking and data representation together dominate Component 1 — plan ~17 article lessons across these three units (over half the unit count) to match weighting.
Boolean algebra is small in mark allocation but high in difficulty — give it a dedicated lesson rather than tucking it inside logic gates.
Component 2 requires Python 3. Practice content should default to Python in examples (matching the on-screen exam) and only use pseudocode for algorithm-design questions.
current_spec_changes: Specification first taught from 2020, first awarded Summer 2022. No subsequent revisions to subject content as of May 2026. Source: WJEC Eduqas GCSE Computer Science Specification (Teaching from 2020), eduqas.co.uk/media/tf3bvmxe/eduqas-gcse-computer-science-specification-10-02-2020.pdf.
Component 2 on-screen examination uses Python 3 only (no additional libraries). Centres receive a scenario on 1 September prior to the award year. Source: Specification section 3.2.
pedagogical_notes: PRIMM (Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make) is the most strongly evidenced approach to teaching GCSE programming in the UK. Practice items in the on-screen unit are structured along PRIMM stages — Predict-the-Output, Investigate-with-Trace, Modify-the-Code, Fix-the-Code. Source: Raspberry Pi Foundation, Sentance et al., 'Teaching computer programming with PRIMM: a sociocultural perspective' (Computer Science Education, 2019), raspberrypi.org/app/uploads/2022/08/Teaching_Programming_with_PRIMM-1.pdf.

CSTA guidance recommends teaching algorithm tracing as an explicit pen-and-paper skill before attempting to debug at the keyboard — trace tables with row-per-line variable state are the highest-leverage practice format for Eduqas Component 1 algorithm questions. Source: CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards, web.ped.nm.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/CSTA-K-12-Computer-Science-Standards-Revised-2017-2.pdf.

Teach Computing (NCCE) GCSE Computer Science pedagogy course recommends paired programming and Parsons problems for early-stage code construction. Build at least one Parsons-style (rearrange-the-lines) drill into each Python practice lesson. Source: teachcomputing.org/courses/CO242/teaching-gcse-computer-science-pedagogy-for-programming.

Cambridge Assessment research on extended-response marking shows students benefit from exemplar paragraphs at each level (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging). For the 8-mark Discuss Impacts question type, embed exemplar paragraphs in revision technique guides. Source: cambridgeassessment.org.uk, Macinska & Benton (2020), 'The usefulness of detailed marks within levels-based mark schemes'.

EEF guidance on Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools recommends explicit teaching of disciplinary writing. Treat 8-mark Discuss-style answers as a writing skill, not a content recall task — model paragraph structure (claim → evidence → counter → judgement). Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk, Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report.

_practice_unit_decision: Practice unit "Python Practice for the On-Screen Exam" was DROPPED on 2026-05-20. Reason: revising on-screen coding from a static web platform is a weak fit (students need a real IDE). Article unit "Algorithms, Programming and Software Development" carries the conceptual load with code blocks + worked traces. Eduqas CS is also a minority board, so the audience-vs-effort case is weak.
